title: What is the difference between class-level and method-level @Transactional?
keyPoints: Class-level @Transactional applies as the default for ALL public methods of the bean
Method-level @Transactional overrides the class-level settings for that specific method
Spring resolves precedence through AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource: method first, then class fallback
Best practice: @Transactional(readOnly = true) on class, writable @Transactional on write methods
New read methods are safe by default because they inherit the class-level readOnly flag
Only public methods are proxied; class-level annotation does not affect private or package-private methods

s1_definition.oneliner: Class-level @Transactional sets the default for all public methods, and method-level @Transactional overrides it for that specific method.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Class-level @Transactional** – applies to every public method in the bean as the default transaction configuration; any method without its own annotation inherits these settings.
- **Method-level @Transactional** – overrides the class-level settings for that one method; Spring's `AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource` checks the method first and falls back to the class.
- **Precedence rule** – method-level always wins over class-level; there is no merging of attributes.
- **Best practice** – set `readOnly = true` at the class level so all query methods skip dirty checking and route to replicas by default, then override with a writable `@Transactional` on the few methods that write data.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the branch door has a sign: "All counters are read-only enquiry by default." This is the class-level annotation. Counter number 3 has its own sign: "This counter handles transfers and deposits." That is the method-level override. If a counter has no sign of its own, it follows the door sign. If it has its own sign, the door sign does not apply to it.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  @Service
  @Transactional(readOnly = true)    ← Class-level default
  public class AccountService {
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                    │
  │  getBalance()     → readOnly=true  (from class)   │
  │  findByCustomer() → readOnly=true  (from class)   │
  │  countActive()    → readOnly=true  (from class)   │
  │                                                    │
  │  @Transactional(rollbackFor=Exception.class)       │
  │  deposit()        → readOnly=false (method wins)   │
  │                                                    │
  │  @Transactional(rollbackFor=Exception.class)       │
  │  withdraw()       → readOnly=false (method wins)   │
  │                                                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Class-level @Transactional applies as the default for all public methods in the service. Method-level @Transactional overrides the class-level settings for that specific method. The override is complete, not a merge: if the method-level annotation specifies only rollbackFor, the other attributes like readOnly and timeout take their default values, not the class-level values.

The best practice at National Bank of India is to set @Transactional(readOnly = true) at the class level because most service methods are read operations like getBalance, getByType, and countActive. The few methods that modify data, like deposit and withdraw, get a method-level @Transactional that overrides back to writable. This ensures that all read methods automatically skip Hibernate dirty checking, can be routed to a read replica, and do not accidentally perform writes. If Rajesh's team adds a new read method and forgets to annotate it, it is safe by default because the class-level readOnly applies.

The key nuance to remember is the no-merging rule. Spring does not combine class-level and method-level attributes. A method-level annotation replaces the entire class-level definition. If the class sets timeout to 30 and the method only sets rollbackFor, the method's timeout is -1 (the default), not 30. Always specify all needed attributes at the method level when overriding.

Remember one sentence: class-level @Transactional is the default for all public methods, method-level overrides it completely (no merging), and the best pattern is readOnly on the class with writable overrides on write methods.
